title: Did Archimedes Really Shout Eureka Naked? The Earliest Record Came Nearly 200 Years Later
description:
You've surely heard it: Archimedes, in the bathtub, figures it out and runs naked into the street shouting Eureka. This file covers only what the records hold, one by one, by date. The earliest text found so far is the preface to Book 9 of the Roman architect Vitruvius's Ten Books on Architecture (De architectura), dedicated to Augustus and written in the late 1st century BC, nearly 200 years after Archimedes: King Hiero's golden crown (really a wreath of gold leaves), a goldsmith accused of mixing in silver, water overflowing in a public bath, and "naked, heading for home" (nudus vadens domum versus), shouting εύρηκα ("I've found it") all the way. The text says "homeward"; there is no "into the street" or "forgot his clothes." None of Archimedes' surviving works, On Floating Bodies included, says a word about a crown or a bathtub; On Floating Bodies is about weighing in water, not overflowing water. Over a century later, Plutarch also wrote of the bath and the cry "I've found it," but says nothing of clothes or of going home, and his word is "walk." A Latin poem from the late Roman Empire, author unknown, has the gold crown but no bath, and uses a balance in water. In 1586, Galileo, in his early 20s, called measuring the water "crude, far from exact" in a short essay shown only to friends (La Bilancetta, "The Little Balance"), and guessed a writer of that era added it himself; in 1589, Giambattista della Porta also found it hard to use, in a printed book. Mathematician Chris Rorres estimated (a 1 kg wreath, 30% silver, a 20 cm opening): the water level differs by only 0.41 mm, but a balance in water differs by 13 g.

Limits: Rorres's numbers are his own assumed scenario; no one can prove the story false, and the naked run home rests on Vitruvius alone, so this file remains open. Sources are listed in the references below.

Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; historical figures are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses; modern researchers are not drawn.

Data as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

ek101.text: Surely you've heard: Archimedes cracked it in the tub, ran naked into the street shouting Eureka.

ek102.text: But the earliest words recording this scene came nearly 200 years after him.

ek103.text: 3rd century BC, Syracuse. Archimedes happens to walk into a public bathhouse.

ek104.text: A hard problem weighs on him.

ek105.text: He sits down in the bath, and the deeper he sinks, the more water spills over.

ek106.text: In that moment, what did he realize?

ek107.text: Stranger yet: over a century later, someone retold this bath, but left one thing out.

ek108.text: Over 1,000 years later, a man in his early 20s read the method and began with harsh words.

ek109.text: This file reads every record of the bath by date: five old texts, one calculation.

ek110.text: Did he really run naked into the street shouting Eureka?

ek201.text: The earliest words I mentioned are in a Roman architect's book.

ek202.text: He was Vitruvius, a military engineer who oversaw catapults for Augustus;

ek203.text: he dedicated his Ten Books on Architecture to Augustus, late in the 1st century BC; the nearly 200 years count from here.

ek204.text: Where did he get this story?

ek205.text: The book doesn't say. Each time I get here, I want to ask him.

ek206.text: The story opens Book 9. Hiero, king of Syracuse, ruled the city for over half a century.

ek207.text: The year he took power, he vowed a golden crown to a temple.

ek208.text: Call it a crown, but it was a wreath of gold leaves; forget the jeweled crown you're picturing.

ek209.text: The king gave a goldsmith gold by weight;

ek210.text: The smith delivered the wreath; on the scale, it matched exactly.

ek212.text: Someone alleged he stole some gold and added equal weight in silver.

ek213.text: But it was meant for the gods: it couldn't be melted or scraped.

ek214.text: Angry as he was, the king couldn't expose it, so he asked Archimedes. And then?

ek215.text: The troubled man walking into the bathhouse at the start? That's him, now.

ek216.text: The overflowing water showed him how to expose it:

ek217.text: An object in water displaces water equal to its size; gold and silver of equal weight differ in size.

ek218.text: Without waiting a moment, he leapt from the bath in joy,

ek219.text: naked, heading for home, shouting loudly as he ran:

ek220.text: Eureka, Eureka! Meaning: I've found it.

ek221.text: So did he run naked through the streets?

ek301.text: The text says "homeward"; it says nothing of streets;

ek302.text: and he ran home from a public bathhouse, not out the door from his own tub.

ek303.text: "Forgot his clothes," "ran all over town": added later, layer by layer.

ek304.text: That's how the street-running version from your childhood grew.

ek305.text: As for "naked": the Latin word sometimes means in just a short tunic;

ek306.text: But he'd just jumped out of a bath; read literally, the most natural sense is naked. On this, I won't cover for him.

ek307.text: At home, how to prove it?

ek308.text: Vitruvius goes on, but first hedges on his own: "it is said."

ek309.text: He reportedly made a gold and a silver block, each the wreath's weight, and put each in a full vessel,

ek310.text: then, with a Roman measure, cup by cup, measured how much water it took to refill it.

ek311.text: The wreath displaced more water than the gold block; so the silver was exposed.

ek313.text: The text is silent; the story stops there.

ek314.text: But why would a book on architecture tell this story?

ek315.text: Because, funnily enough, Book 9 opens with a protest on writers' behalf:

ek316.text: Writers deserve the glory athletes get, and even more.

ek317.text: Archimedes is one of his examples; the one before is Pythagoras.

ek318.text: The hero himself? Did Archimedes ever write of this wreath?

ek401.text: At least in his surviving works, there's no word of a crown, nor a bathtub.

ek402.text: In 1897, British scholar Heath edited his complete works in English;

ek403.text: Cover to cover, "crown" appears only in the editor's own intro and notes;

ek404.text: and for On Floating Bodies, he had only a Latin translation.

ek405.text: Some of his books were lost; some survived by sheer luck. How lucky?

ek406.text: The Greek original of On Floating Bodies turned up later in a parchment scraped and written over.

ek407.text: And On Floating Bodies is about exactly what happens to things in water.

ek408.text: It says: anything heavier than water weighs less in water,

ek409.text: by exactly the weight of the water it displaces.

ek410.text: That's the buoyancy from your textbook. The catch: he's describing weighing in water.

ek411.text: But the overflowing bath from the start compares volume, not this book's principle.

ek412.text: When I first read this, I froze too.

ek413.text: How did other ancients tell of this bath?

ek501.text: That version from over a century later is by the Greek writer Plutarch.

ek502.text: He hedges first with "it is said": by his day, it was already a story going around.

ek503.text: Reportedly, while bathing, Archimedes saw in the overflow how to measure the crown;

ek504.text: as if possessed, he leapt out crying "I've found it!" and walked off crying it.

ek505.text: He tells it to mock gluttons: nobody ever heard of a gourmet finishing a meal and shouting "I've eaten!"

ek506.text: Last great meal: did you run out yelling?

ek508.text: So what was the one thing left out?

ek509.text: It's the nakedness: Plutarch says not one word about clothes;

ek510.text: nor that he went home; his word is "walk," not "run."

ek511.text: Elsewhere, Plutarch writes he was often dragged off to be bathed and oiled, and drew geometry in the oil on his body.

ek512.text: No wonder the story fits him so neatly; that's my guess.

ek513.text: A bath, but no nakedness; any version the other way around?

ek514.text: Yes. A Latin poem from the late Roman Empire, author unknown, clearly tells the same story:

ek515.text: Sicily's king, a gold crown for a god, a smith adding silver: all there;

ek516.text: but no bath, and no one shouting "I've found it";

ek517.text: it doesn't even name Archimedes, just "the master of Syracuse."

ek518.text: Oddly, the three versions even disagree on whom the crown was for:

ek519.text: Vitruvius says the gods, the poem says the king of the gods, and Plutarch doesn't say at all.

ek520.text: The poem uses a balance: equal weights of gold and silver on each pan, balanced,

ek521.text: then into the water together; once submerged, the gold side sinks at once.

ek522.text: Same crown: one way measures water, the other weighs. Which one actually works?

ek601.text: The water-measuring method was already criticized in 1586.

ek602.text: The critic was that man in his early 20s from the start: Italy's Galileo.

ek603.text: He showed a short essay only to friends, unprinted in his life; later called La Bilancetta.

ek605.text: Some write of dunking the crown and telling gold from silver by the rise;

ek606.text: frankly, that's a crude method, far from exact.

ek607.text: He says "some write," but names no one.

ek608.text: So where did the water-measuring come from?

ek609.text: His guess: word spread that Archimedes exposed a gold theft with water; a writer of that era wrote it down,

ek610.text: and, to pad the little he'd heard, added the water-measuring method himself.

ek611.text: We think it's the best line in this whole file.

ek612.text: Still, it's his guess, not evidence; and he doubted only the method, not the bath.

ek613.text: Beyond friends, did anyone print this doubt?

ek614.text: Yes. Three years later, in 1589, another Italian, in a printed book, also called the method difficult;

ek615.text: and said his own method deserved a cry of "Super-Eureka."

ek616.text: So what did Galileo think Archimedes really used?

ek617.text: A balance. Just like that poem: weighing in water.

ek618.text: Remember On Floating Bodies? Galileo said Archimedes would've used this,

ek619.text: since it rests on the very principle that book proves.

ek620.text: You may wonder: crude or not, how far off can measuring water be?

ek701.text: Mathematician Rorres worked it out. His first assumption: a 1 kg wreath.

ek702.text: The largest gold wreath of that era ever unearthed is just over 700 g; rounding to 1 kg seems fair to me.

ek703.text: 30% of the gold was swapped for silver; the container's mouth is 20 cm across.

ek704.text: Put in the wreath, then equal-weight gold, and the levels differ by just:

ek705.text: 0.41 millimeters, less than half a millimeter.

ek706.text: The extra water isn't small, about the size of three dice;

ek707.text: but drop three dice into a basin of water, and the surface barely moves.

ek708.text: And with a balance, weighing in water?

ek709.text: The sides differ by 13 grams; he says scales of Archimedes' time could easily tell.

ek710.text: In 2006, he told Scientific American: measuring water works in theory;

ek711.text: but in practice, reality gets in the way.

ek712.text: He named three spoilers: surface tension, water clinging when it's lifted out, bubbles in the wreath's gaps.

ek713.text: The method likely fails; what of the bath and the "I've found it"?

ek714.text: Rorres says there may be some truth to it: Archimedes did measure the volume of things;

ek715.text: but that "I've found it" moment was maybe due to his discovery of buoyancy,

ek716.text: not the tub, then a naked dash through the streets.

ek717.text: So, the opening question: did he really run naked into the street shouting Eureka?

ek718.text: The naked run home survives in just one record, by that Roman architect;

ek719.text: whether it really happened, no evidence can answer.

ek721.text: In your childhood version, was Archimedes dressed as he ran out? Tell me below.

ek722.text: This channel tells only what records hold. Subscribe to open files with us.
